planet.title: Planet and health
planet.summary: The living systems everyone depends on: a stable climate, working ecosystems, enough food and clean water, and protection from disease. The map shows how damage to one feeds into the others.

power.title: Power and democracy
power.summary: Who holds power and how it is used: the health of democratic institutions, the rise of authoritarian politics, the concentration of wealth, and how societies respond to people who move.

information.title: Information and technology
information.summary: How people come to know what is true, and the technology that shapes it: misleading information, organised campaigns to create doubt, the platforms where news spreads, artificial intelligence and surveillance.

826.name: United Kingdom
826.summary: The UK has more than halved its greenhouse gas emissions since 1990, yet its climate is visibly changing and its wildlife is still declining. More than a quarter of children live in relative poverty once housing costs are counted, trust in government is at a record low, and economists disagree about how much leaving the EU has cost.

claims.text: The UK's greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 were 53% lower than in 1990, and 3% lower than in 2023. The country's last coal-fired power station closed in September 2024.
claims.note: Official statistics. They count only emissions produced inside the UK, not those from making the goods it imports.

quotes.text: In 2024, total greenhouse gas emissions were estimated to be 373 MtCO2e, a decrease of 11 MtCO2e (3%) from the 2023 estimate of 384 MtCO2e. In 2024 they were 53% lower than they were in 1990.
the closure of the UK’s last coal-fired power station in September 2024.

claims.text: The UK is warming. The decade 2015–2024 was 1.24°C warmer than 1961–1990, and sea levels around the UK have risen by about 19.5 cm since 1901, two-thirds of that in the last three decades.
claims.note: From the Met Office's annual, peer-reviewed report on the UK climate, built on long instrumental records.

claims.text: Across 753 land and freshwater species tracked since 1970, UK wildlife has fallen in abundance by 19% on average. About one in six species is at risk of being lost from Great Britain.
claims.note: Compiled by about 50 conservation and research organisations from monitoring data. Long-term data exist for only a fraction of species.

quotes.text: The abundance of 753 terrestrial and freshwater species has on average fallen by 19% across the UK since 1970.
Nearly one in six species are threatened with extinction from Great Britain

claims.text: In 2024–25, 27% of UK children lived in relative poverty once housing costs are taken into account, meaning their household income was below 60% of the typical (median) income.
claims.note: Official statistics from a large household survey. Relative poverty measures how far incomes fall below typical incomes, not hardship directly.

quotes.text: With rates of low income displayed to the nearest per cent, relative low income BHC was 21% and AHC 27% in FYE 2025, compared with 20% and 28% the previous year.
A household is said to be in relative low income if their net equivalised disposable household income is below a threshold set at 60% of median income that year

claims.text: In 2024 only 12% of people in Britain trusted governments to put the nation's interests above their party's 'just about always' or 'most of the time', the lowest since the question was first asked in 1986, when it was 40%. 46% said they 'almost never' did.
claims.note: British Social Attitudes is a long-running survey of a random sample of the public.

quotes.text: only 12% say that they trust government “just about always” or “most of the time” (a new record low) while 46% indicate they “almost never” trust the government (also the highest on record).
Table 8, Level of trust in British governments, 1986–2024. Just about always/Most of the time, 1986: 40%

claims.text: The V-Dem Institute lists the UK among ten countries that began moving away from democracy in 2025. The UK still ranks 30th of 179 countries on V-Dem's Liberal Democracy Index.
claims.note: The report does not say which UK measures declined, and a new episode of decline can stop or reverse. V-Dem's scores rest partly on expert judgement; see the debate under Authoritarianism and the far right.

quotes.text: 10 new autocratizers identified in 2025. Among the new autocratizers are five European countries: Croatia, Italy, Slovakia, Slovenia, and the UK.
Table A2, Liberal Democracy Index 2025. United Kingdom: rank 30, score 0.69

debates.question: How much has leaving the EU cost the UK economy?
debates.agreed: Leaving the EU raised the cost of trading with the UK's largest trading partner, and most economists expect this to leave the UK somewhat poorer over time. The dispute is over how large the effect is, and whether it can be separated from Covid, the energy price shock and other events since 2016.

positions.label: A large cost, already visible
positions.text: Bloom and colleagues combine a survey of UK businesses with estimates from economy-wide data. They estimate that by the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, investment by 12% to 13%, and both employment and productivity by 3% to 4%. Their paper is a working paper and has not yet been peer reviewed.

quotes.text: we combine estimates using macro data with estimates using micro data collected through our Decision Maker Panel survey. These suggest that by the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, with the impact accumulating steadily over time. We estimate that investment was reduced by 12% to 13%, employment by 3% to 4% and productivity by 3% to 4%.

positions.label: A smaller long-run cost
positions.text: The Office for Budget Responsibility, the UK's official forecaster, assumes Brexit will leave productivity 4% lower in the long run than if the UK had stayed in the EU, with exports and imports both around 15% lower.

quotes.text: will reduce long-run productivity by 4 per cent relative to remaining in the EU.
Both exports and imports will be around 15 per cent lower in the long run than if the UK had remained in the EU.

positions.label: Too early to measure reliably
positions.text: Gudgin argues that comparing the UK with a blend of similar economies is a flawed method. In 2022 he found no sign that UK growth had lagged behind the G7, judged the wider effect on GDP likely to be small, and said more time was needed for an accurate assessment. He wrote this before the newer estimates above.

quotes.text: Analysis by Policy Exchange argues that the CER’s doppelgänger methodology is fatally flawed and its conclusion of a large hit to the UK’s economic performance is incorrect. In a direct comparison with G7 countries there is no sign that the UK has lagged behind in growth of GDP.

the fact that UK exports to the EU have held up well suggests that any wider impact on GDP is in fact likely to be small. More time and patience are needed to make an accurate assessment of the economic impact of Brexit

agreedQuotes.text: This largely reflects our view that the increase in non-tariff barriers on UK-EU trade acts as an additional impediment to the exploitation of comparative advantage. In order to generate this figure, we looked at a range of external estimates of the effect of leaving
These suggest that by the end of 2025 Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, with the impact accumulating steadily over time.

summaryQuotes.text: In 2024 they were 53% lower than they were in 1990.
Across the UK species studied have declined on average by 19% since 1970.
relative low income BHC was 21% and AHC 27% in FYE 2025
Just 12% trust governments to put the interests of the nation above those of their own party just about always or most of the time, a record low.
will reduce long-run productivity by 4 per cent relative to remaining in the EU.

840.name: United States
840.summary: The United States has put more carbon dioxide into the air than any other country, and is warming faster than the world as a whole. Wealth is more concentrated at the top than at any point since the Federal Reserve's records began in 1989, Americans die younger than people in other rich countries, and the country's democracy scores fell sharply in 2025.

claims.text: Since 1850 the United States has emitted more carbon dioxide than any other country: about a fifth of the world total, nearly twice the share of China, which is second.
claims.note: Carbon Brief analysis of Global Carbon Project and other datasets, covering 1850–2021 and including emissions from land use. Shares shift slightly with the data and years used.

quotes.text: the US has released more than 509GtCO2 since 1850 and is responsible for the largest share of historical emissions, Carbon Brief analysis shows, with some 20% of the global total.
China is a relatively distant second, with 11%

claims.text: Since 1970 the lower 48 states have warmed by about 1.4°C (2.5°F) and Alaska by about 2.3°C (4.2°F), compared with about 0.9°C (1.7°F) for the world as a whole.
claims.note: From the Fifth National Climate Assessment, the US government's official review of climate science, published in 2023.

claims.text: The richest 1% of US households held 32.5% of all household wealth in mid-2026, up from 22.8% in 1989. The poorer half of households held 2.3%.
claims.note: Federal Reserve estimates that combine its household wealth survey with the national accounts. How much income inequality has risen is debated; see Economic inequality and concentrated wealth.

quotes.text: Share of Net Worth Held by the Top 1% (99th to 100th Wealth Percentiles): 22.8% in 1989 Q3 (the first observation); 32.5% in 2026 Q2
Share of Net Worth Held by the Bottom 50% (1st to 50th Wealth Percentiles): 2.3% in 2026 Q2

claims.text: Americans die younger than people in other rich countries. Had the US matched the death rates of other high-income countries, about 705,000 fewer Americans would have died in 2023. These excess deaths made up 46% of all deaths under age 65.
claims.note: Peer-reviewed and free to read. Results depend somewhat on which countries are compared. The authors point to drug overdoses, gun deaths and heart and metabolic disease as likely causes.

quotes.text: Excess deaths attributable to the US mortality disadvantage peaked at 1 008 369 in 2020 and 1 098 808 in 2021, then declined to 820 396 in 2022 and 705 331 in 2023.
In 2023, excess US deaths accounted for 22.9% of all deaths and 46.0% of deaths among US residents younger than 65 years

claims.text: Over four decades, hostility between supporters of opposing parties rose more in the United States than in any of eleven other wealthy democracies studied.
claims.note: Built from 149 election surveys. Question wording varies between countries and years, which limits precision.

quotes.text: We measure trends in affective polarization in twelve OECD countries over the past four decades. According to our baseline estimates, the United States experienced the largest increase in polarization over this period.

claims.text: In 2025 the US score on V-Dem's Liberal Democracy Index fell by 24% in one year, and its world rank dropped from 20th to 51st of 179. V-Dem calls the speed of the decline unprecedented in modern times, and points to power being concentrated in the presidency and checks and balances being undercut.
claims.note: Election measures were not re-scored in 2025, as there was no national election. V-Dem's scores rest partly on expert judgement; see the debate under Authoritarianism and the far right.

quotes.text: The scale and speed of autocratization under the Trump administration are unprecedented in modern times. Within one year, the USA’s LDI score has declined by 24%; its world rank dropped from 20th to 51st place out of 179 nations.
Trump’s second term can be summarized as a rapid and aggressive concentration of powers in the presidency.

summaryQuotes.text: the US has released more than 509GtCO2 since 1850 and is responsible for the largest share of historical emissions, Carbon Brief analysis shows, with some 20% of the global total.
Share of Net Worth Held by the Top 1% (99th to 100th Wealth Percentiles): 22.8% in 1989 Q3 (the first observation); 32.5% in 2026 Q2
In 2023, excess US deaths accounted for 22.9% of all deaths and 46.0% of deaths among US residents younger than 65 years
Within one year, the USA’s LDI score has declined by 24%; its world rank dropped from 20th to 51st place out of 179 nations.

climate-change.title: Climate change
climate-change.summary: The planet is heating because of greenhouse gases from burning coal, oil and gas, and from changes in how land is used. The basic science is not in doubt. The live questions are how fast emissions can fall and how the costs are shared.

claims.text: Human activity has caused the global warming seen since the industrial era: about 1.1°C by 2011–2020, compared with 1850–1900.
claims.note: The IPCC, which reviews the whole field for the world's governments, calls this unequivocal. A separate review of more than 88,000 climate papers found over 99% agreement.

quotes.text: Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020.

We conclude with high statistical confidence that the scientific consensus on human-caused contemporary climate change—expressed as a proportion of the total publications—exceeds 99% in the peer reviewed scientific literature.

claims.text: Every additional increment of warming brings greater risks, losses and damage.
claims.note: The IPCC gives this its top confidence rating.

quotes.text: Risks and projected adverse impacts and related losses and damages from climate change escalate with every increment of global warming (very high confidence).

claims.text: Countries' climate pledges as they stood in late 2021 make it likely that warming will pass 1.5°C this century.
claims.note: This is a projection, so the outcome depends on what governments do next. The assessment behind it is robust.

quotes.text: Global GHG emissions in 2030 implied by nationally determined contributions (NDCs) announced by October 2021 make it likely that warming will exceed 1.5°C during the 21st century and make it harder to limit warming below 2°C.

debates.question: Can rich economies keep growing while cutting emissions fast enough?
debates.agreed: Emissions have to fall quickly. In 18 developed economies they did fall between 2005 and 2015. The dispute is whether that can happen fast enough, everywhere, while economies keep growing.

positions.label: Green growth is unlikely to be enough
positions.text: Hickel and Kallis review past trends and model projections. They conclude that cutting carbon fast enough to stay under 1.5°C or 2°C while GDP keeps growing is highly unlikely, and that there is no evidence resource use can be separated from growth at a global scale.

quotes.text: we find that: (1) there is no empirical evidence that absolute decoupling from resource use can be achieved on a global scale against a background of continued economic growth, and (2) absolute decoupling from carbon emissions is highly unlikely to be achieved at a rate rapid enough to prevent global warming over 1.5°C or 2°C, even under optimistic policy conditions.

positions.label: Cuts alongside growth are already happening
positions.text: Le Quéré and colleagues show emissions falling in 18 developed economies as renewables displaced fossil fuels and energy use dropped. They add that slower economic growth explains part of the fall, and that much stronger policy is still needed.

quotes.text: We show that within this group, the displacement of fossil fuels by renewable energy and decreases in energy use explain decreasing CO2 emissions. However, the decrease in energy use can be explained at least in part by a lower growth in gross domestic product.
these efforts need to be maintained and enhanced by more stringent policy actions

agreedQuotes.text: All global modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot, and those that limit warming to 2°C (>67%), involve rapid and deep and, in most cases, immediate greenhouse gas emissions reductions in all sectors this decade.
Here we analyse the drivers of decreasing CO2 emissions in a group of 18 developed economies that have decarbonized over the period 2005–2015.

summaryQuotes.text: Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020. Global greenhouse gas emissions have continued to increase, with unequal historical and ongoing contributions arising from unsustainable energy use, land use and land-use change, lifestyles and patterns of consumption and production

We conclude with high statistical confidence that the scientific consensus on human-caused contemporary climate change—expressed as a proportion of the total publications—exceeds 99% in the peer reviewed scientific literature.

ecological-breakdown.title: Ecological breakdown
ecological-breakdown.summary: Wild species, and the ecosystems people rely on for food, water and a stable climate, are declining worldwide. Climate change is one cause among several. The biggest causes so far are how we use land and sea, and how much we take from them.

claims.text: Around one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades.
claims.note: From the IPBES global assessment. The figure is an estimate scaled up from the groups studied in detail. The insect share is the least certain part.

quotes.text: around 1 million species already face extinction, many within decades, unless action is taken to reduce the intensity of drivers of biodiversity loss.
quotes.where: Summary for Policymakers, key message A

claims.text: The main direct causes of nature loss, in order of impact so far, are: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation of wildlife, climate change, pollution, and invasive species.
claims.note: This ranking comes from the IPBES global assessment, whose summary was approved by its member governments.

quotes.text: The direct drivers of change in nature with the largest global impact have been (starting with those with most impact): changes in land and sea use; direct exploitation of organisms; climate change; pollution; and invasion of alien species.
quotes.where: Summary for Policymakers, key message B

claims.text: Seven of the nine planetary boundaries that scientists use to track Earth's stability have been crossed. Ocean acidification joined the list in 2025.
claims.note: The measurements behind each boundary are solid. Where exactly to draw each safe limit involves scientific judgement, so read the count as a well-supported indicator, not a precise threshold.

quotes.text: The 2025 PHC report concludes that seven out of nine Planetary Boundaries have been breached, with all of those seven showing trends of increasing pressure
This means that, for the first time, we assess that the Planetary Boundary for Ocean Acidification has been transgressed.

This planetary boundaries framework update finds that six of the nine boundaries are transgressed, suggesting that Earth is now well outside of the safe operating space for humanity. Ocean acidification is close to being breached

summaryQuotes.text: The direct drivers of change in nature with the largest global impact have been (starting with those with most impact): changes in land and sea use; direct exploitation of organisms; climate change; pollution; and invasion of alien species.
summaryQuotes.where: Summary for Policymakers, key message B

ai-development.title: AI development
ai-development.summary: General-purpose AI systems are improving quickly and being built into work, media and public services. Both the benefits and the harms are real, and much of the evidence is still coming in.

claims.text: General-purpose AI keeps getting more capable, most visibly in mathematics, coding and working on tasks without supervision.
claims.note: A finding of the International AI Safety Report 2026, written by more than 100 experts and backed by over 30 countries and international organisations.

quotes.text: General-purpose AI capabilities have continued to improve, especially in mathematics, coding, and autonomous operation.

claims.text: Today's systems still fail in ways such as inventing facts, writing faulty code and giving misleading advice. Current techniques reduce these failures, but not to the level needed where the stakes are high.
claims.note: Same report. Documented across many systems.

quotes.text: Current AI systems sometimes exhibit failures such as fabricating information, producing flawed code, and giving misleading advice.
Current techniques can reduce failure rates but not to the level required in many high-stakes settings.

claims.text: So far there is no effect on overall employment, though there are some signs of falling demand for early-career workers in some of the jobs most exposed to AI.
claims.note: The data cover only a few years, and effects may take time to show.

quotes.text: Early evidence shows no effect on overall employment, but some signs of declining demand for early-career workers in some AI-exposed occupations, such as writing.

debates.question: How much electricity will AI need?
debates.agreed: Data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of the world's electricity, and demand is rising.

positions.label: Central projection
positions.text: The IEA's base case has data-centre demand more than doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030 and reaching roughly 1,200 TWh by 2035.

quotes.text: Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030.
our Base Case sees global data centre electricity consumption rising to around 1 200 TWh by 2035.

positions.label: A wide range is possible
positions.text: Across the IEA's scenarios, demand in 2035 runs from 700 to 1,700 TWh. Stronger gains in the efficiency of AI hardware and models pull it down. Faster uptake of AI pushes it up.

quotes.text: By 2035, the range of data centre electricity demand across our cases spans from 700 to 1 700 TWh.
A Lift-Off Case assumes higher rates of AI uptake and proactive action to reduce energy sector bottlenecks.

Our High Efficiency Case highlights the potential for even stronger gains in the efficiency of AI-related hardware and AI models. In this case, electricity demand from data centres is 20% lower in 2035 than in the Base Case.

agreedQuotes.text: Data centres accounted for around 1.5% of the world’s electricity consumption in 2024, or 415 terawatt-hours (TWh).

summaryQuotes.text: General-purpose AI systems have also continued to diffuse, faster than many previous technologies in some places, though unevenly across countries and regions.
Real-world evidence for several risks is growing

authoritarianism-far-right.title: Authoritarianism and the far right
authoritarianism-far-right.summary: Many researchers report that elected governments in a growing number of countries are weakening courts, the press and civil rights, and that far-right parties have gained ground in many democracies. How large the shift is, and what to call it, are both debated.

claims.text: By the V-Dem Institute's count, 74% of the world's people lived in autocracies at the end of 2025, up from 50% in 2005. Only 7% lived in liberal democracies.
claims.note: V-Dem is the largest academic democracy dataset. Its scores rest partly on expert judgement, which is the subject of a debate below.

quotes.text: 74% of the world population (6 billion) now live in autocracies.
Only 7% of the world population (0.6 billion) live in liberal democracies.
SHARE OF WORLD POPULATION LIVING IN AUTOCRACIES 2005: 50% 2025: 74%

claims.text: 44 countries were moving toward autocracy in 2025. They are home to 41% of the world's population, a record.
claims.note: Same dataset, same caveat.

quotes.text: Nearly a quarter of the world’s nations are now on the list of autocratizers: 44 countries.
A record of 41% (3.4 billion) of the world population currently reside in autocratizing countries.

claims.text: Since around 2000, far-right parties and ideas have moved from the margins into the mainstream of many democracies.
claims.note: The central argument of Mudde's survey of the research on far-right parties.

debates.question: How much democratic decline is really happening?
debates.agreed: Some countries have clearly become less democratic. The dispute is about the size of the global trend.

positions.label: Expert-coded indices show a large decline
positions.text: V-Dem's 2026 report finds democracy for the average person back at 1978 levels. The V-Dem team argue that their expert-based method limits the potential for bias, and that today's backsliding works through subtle damage to civil liberties, the press and the courts, which is harder to observe than a rigged election.

quotes.text: Democracy is back to 1978 levels for the average global citizen.
The second section describes how V-Dem’s expert-based approach to measuring democracy limits the potential for systematic bias

This leads to a more subtle degrading of less formalized and more difficult to observe supporting pillars of democracy, including civil liberties, civil society mobilization, freedom of the press, and judicial independence.

positions.label: Objective indicators show little decline
positions.text: Little and Meng look at measures that need no judgement, such as whether incumbents lose elections. Over the decade they studied they find little evidence of global decline. They consider whether expert coders are biased, and accept that democracy could be eroding in ways only judgement can detect, but say the existing evidence does not justify that claim.

quotes.text: Our study surveys objective indicators of democracy (e.g., incumbent performance in elections) and finds little evidence of global democratic decline during the past decade. To explain the discrepancy in trends between expert-coded and objective indicators, we consider the role of coder bias and leaders strategically using more subtle undemocratic action. Although we cannot rule out the possibility that the world is becoming less democratic exclusively in ways that require subjective judgment to detect, this claim is not justified by existing evidence.

agreedQuotes.text: Although it is true that in recent years some countries have become less democratic and others have become more democratic, this has always been true.
During the past decade, analyses drawing on several democracy measures have shown a global trend of democratic retrenchment.

debates.question: Is "fascism" the right word for today's far right?
debates.agreed: Scholars on both sides describe today's far right as nativist and authoritarian. The dispute is whether the historical term fits, and whether using it helps.

positions.label: Mostly no: "radical right" is more accurate
positions.text: Mudde separates the extreme right, which rejects democracy outright and includes fascism, from the radical right, which accepts elections but opposes liberal-democratic limits such as minority rights and independent courts. On this view most successful far-right parties today are radical right, and calling them fascist hides how they work.

positions.label: Sometimes yes: judge movements by what they do
positions.text: Paxton defines fascism by behaviour, not doctrine: a mass nationalist movement fixated on national decline and victimhood that abandons democratic liberties and turns to violence against its chosen enemies. Scholars who take this approach argue the label applies wherever that pattern appears.

summaryQuotes.text: The world has never before seen as many countries autocratizing at the same time as during the last few years of the “third wave of autocratization”.
Our study surveys objective indicators of democracy (e.g., incumbent performance in elections) and finds little evidence of global democratic decline during the past decade.

misinformation.title: Misinformation
misinformation.summary: False and misleading claims spread through social media, broadcast media and politics. How common they are, and how much they change what people believe or do, are argued over by researchers.

claims.text: On Twitter between 2006 and 2017, fact-checked false stories spread farther, faster and to more people than fact-checked true ones. People, not bots, drove the difference.
claims.note: One large study of about 126,000 stories on one platform. Whether it holds for online information in general is disputed; see the debate below.

quotes.text: We investigated the differential diffusion of all of the verified true and false news stories distributed on Twitter from 2006 to 2017.
Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information
robots accelerated the spread of true and false news at the same rate, implying that false news spreads more than the truth because humans, not robots, are more likely to spread it.

claims.text: People are more often uninformed than misinformed, and surveys tend to overstate how many hold false beliefs.
claims.note: Argued by Altay, Berriche and Acerbi in a review of the field. Other researchers treat misinformation as a larger driver of false belief.

quotes.text: people are more likely to be uninformed than misinformed; surveys overestimate misperceptions and say little about the causal influence of misinformation.

debates.question: Does falsehood really spread faster than truth online?
debates.agreed: In the Twitter dataset, false stories out-travelled true ones. The question is what that says about the wider information environment.

positions.label: Yes, and human psychology explains it
positions.text: Vosoughi, Roy and Aral found the effect in every category of news, strongest for politics. False stories were more novel, and replies to them showed fear, disgust and surprise. They suggest novelty makes people more likely to share.

quotes.text: the effects were more pronounced for false political news than for false news about terrorism, natural disasters, science, urban legends, or financial information. We found that false news was more novel than true news, which suggests that people were more likely to share novel information. Whereas false stories inspired fear, disgust, and surprise in replies, true stories inspired anticipation, sadness, joy, and trust.

positions.label: It depends on what you count
positions.text: Altay, Berriche and Acerbi argue that results change with how misinformation is defined, that the internet is full of memes and entertainment more than news or falsehood, and that misinformation often reaches people who already agree with it.

quotes.text: Second, the internet is not rife with misinformation or news, but with memes and entertaining content. Third, falsehoods do not spread faster than the truth; how we define (mis)information influences our results and their practical implications.
the influence of misinformation on people’s behavior is overblown as misinformation often “preaches to the choir.”

agreedQuotes.text: Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information
how we define (mis)information influences our results and their practical implications.

summaryQuotes.text: Alarmist narratives about online misinformation continue to gain traction despite evidence that its prevalence and impact are overstated.
Falsehood diffused significantly farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth in all categories of information

economic-inequality.title: Economic inequality and concentrated wealth
economic-inequality.summary: Income and, even more, wealth are concentrated among a small share of the world's people. How concentrated is measured in different ways, and the methods are argued over. The pattern matters for who causes emissions, who bears the costs of change, and possibly for how people vote.

claims.text: The richest 10% of people own about three-quarters of the world's wealth. The poorer half own about 2%.
claims.note: From the World Inequality Report 2026, built from tax records, surveys and national accounts. Wealth at the very top is hard to observe, so these are estimates.

quotes.text: Wealth is even more concentrated: the top 10% own three-quarters of global wealth, while the bottom half holds only 2%.

claims.text: Income is less concentrated than wealth but still very unequal. The top 10% of earners receive more than the other 90% put together, and the poorer half receive less than 10% of global income.
claims.note: Same report.

quotes.text: the top 10% of the global population’s income-earners earn more than the remaining 90%, while the poorest half of the global population captures less than 10% of the total global income.

claims.text: Fewer than 60,000 people, the richest 0.001%, hold about three times as much wealth as the poorer half of humanity combined. Their share has grown from almost 4% of global wealth in 1995 to more than 6%.
claims.note: Same report. Estimates for so small a group carry the widest margins.

quotes.text: the wealthiest 0.001% alone, fewer than 60,000 multi-millionaires, control today three times more wealth than half of humanity combined. Their share has grown steadily from almost 4% in 1995 to over 6% today

debates.question: Has the top 1%'s share of US income really surged?
debates.agreed: Tax returns alone give an incomplete picture of top incomes. The dispute is over income that tax returns miss, and who it belongs to.

positions.label: The rise is much smaller than usually claimed
positions.text: Auten and Splinter adjust tax data for changes in tax rules, social changes and missing income. They find that top income shares before tax are lower, and have risen less since 1980, than other studies of tax data show, and that top shares after taxes and transfers have changed little.

quotes.text: Our analysis of pretax income shows that top income shares are lower and have increased less since 1980 than other studies using tax data. In addition, increasing government transfers and tax progressivity have resulted in rising real incomes for all income groups and little change in aftertax top income shares.

positions.label: The rise is large, and the lower estimate rests on doubtful assumptions
positions.text: Piketty, Saez and Zucman reply that the lower figures depend on how untaxed business and capital income is shared out. They argue that once those assumptions are checked against other evidence, the estimates come back close to their own in both level and trend.

quotes.text: We trace the remaining difference with the top 1% income share of Piketty, Saez and Zucman (2018) to assumptions made by Auten and Splinter (2024) about the distribution of untaxed business income, untaxed capital income, and non-cash, notional income. After clarifying these assumptions and confronting them to existing evidence, the Auten and Splinter (2024) estimates become similar in level and trend to those of Piketty, Saez and Zucman (2018).

agreedQuotes.text: Estimates of top income shares based only on individual tax returns are biased by tax-base changes, social changes, and missing income sources.
Auten and Splinter (2024) provide estimates of income inequality in the United States, starting with income observed in tax returns and making adjustments to account for untaxed income.

summaryQuotes.text: Wealth is even more concentrated: the top 10% own three-quarters of global wealth, while the bottom half holds only 2%.
Estimates of top income shares based only on individual tax returns are biased by tax-base changes, social changes, and missing income sources.
I find that the bottom 50% of the world population emitted 12% of global emissions in 2019, whereas the top 10% emitted 48% of the total.

climate-obstruction.title: Organised climate obstruction
climate-obstruction.summary: Some fossil fuel companies and allied organisations have worked to cast doubt on climate science and to slow climate policy. The best-documented case is ExxonMobil, whose own scientists predicted warming accurately while its public messaging stressed uncertainty.

claims.text: Between 1977 and 2003, ExxonMobil's own scientists made global warming projections that proved accurate: 63–83% of them matched the warming later observed.
claims.note: A peer-reviewed analysis in Science of every known projection in the company's internal documents and published papers. The projections were as skilful as those of academic and government models.

quotes.text: we find that 63 to 83% of the climate projections reported by ExxonMobil scientists were accurate in predicting subsequent global warming.

claims.text: ExxonMobil said different things to different audiences. About four in five of its scientific papers and internal documents accepted that climate change is real and human-caused, while 81% of its newspaper advertorials expressed doubt.
claims.note: A content analysis of 187 company documents from 1977 to 2014. Coding text involves judgement, which the authors acknowledge.

quotes.text: 83% of peer-reviewed papers and 80% of internal documents acknowledge that climate change is real and human-caused, yet only 12% of advertorials do so, with 81% instead expressing doubt.

claims.text: In the United States, 91 organisations opposing climate action had a combined income of just over $900 million a year between 2003 and 2010. The study found a trend toward hiding where the money came from, through funds that pass on donations without naming the donors.
claims.note: From tax filings. The figure is these organisations' total income for all their work, not only climate, so it is an upper bound on climate-related spending.

quotes.text: An examination of these data shows that these 91 CCCM organizations have an annual income of just over $900 million, with an annual average of $64 million in identifiable foundation support.
there is evidence of a trend toward concealing the sources of CCCM funding through the use of donor directed philanthropies.

summaryQuotes.text: We find that most of their projections accurately forecast warming that is consistent with subsequent observations.
We conclude that ExxonMobil contributed to advancing climate science—by way of its scientists’ academic publications—but promoted doubt about it in advertorials.
This paper conducts an analysis of the financial resource mobilization of the organizations that make up the climate change counter-movement (CCCM) in the United States.

polarisation-trust.title: Polarisation and trust in institutions
polarisation-trust.summary: In some countries, supporters of opposing parties have come to dislike and distrust each other more, and in many countries fewer than half of people trust their national government. The picture differs sharply from country to country, and what exactly has polarised is debated.

claims.text: Hostility between supporters of opposing parties has not risen everywhere. Across twelve wealthy democracies over four decades it rose most in the United States, rose less in five others and fell in six.
claims.note: Built from 149 election surveys. Question wording varies between countries and years, which limits precision.

quotes.text: We measure trends in affective polarization in twelve OECD countries over the past four decades. According to our baseline estimates, the United States experienced the largest increase in polarization over this period. Five countries experienced a smaller increase in polarization. Six countries experienced a decrease in polarization.

claims.text: Across 30 OECD countries in 2023, 39% of people had high or moderately high trust in their national government and 44% had low or no trust.
claims.note: From a survey of nearly 60,000 people. Trust in the police, courts and civil service was higher than trust in national government.

debates.question: Is polarisation about policy views or about feelings?
debates.agreed: In the United States, partisans' dislike of the other side has grown. The dispute is over what has happened to ordinary voters' views on policy.

positions.label: Mostly feelings
positions.text: Iyengar and colleagues describe a divide rooted in party as a social identity: ordinary Americans increasingly dislike and distrust people from the other party. They treat this as a different thing from disagreement over issues.

quotes.text: While previously polarization was primarily seen only in issue-based terms, a new type of division has emerged in the mass public in recent years: Ordinary Americans increasingly dislike and distrust those from the other party.
We trace its origins to the power of partisanship as a social identity

positions.label: Most voters are still moderate
positions.text: Fiorina and colleagues argue that polarisation is largely confined to politicians and activists. On this view most Americans hold moderate views, and they only appear polarised because they are offered more extreme choices.

positions.label: Policy views have polarised too
positions.text: Abramowitz and Saunders use election surveys to argue that Democratic and Republican voters' beliefs have grown much further apart since the 1970s, most of all among the best informed and most politically active.

agreedQuotes.text: Ordinary Americans increasingly dislike and distrust those from the other party.

summaryQuotes.text: According to our baseline estimates, the United States experienced the largest increase in polarization over this period. Five countries experienced a smaller increase in polarization. Six countries experienced a decrease in polarization.

platform-media-power.title: Platform and media power
platform-media-power.summary: Social media platforms now carry much of the political news people see, and a handful of companies decide how it is ranked. Researchers have begun to test how far the design of those feeds shapes what people believe, with mixed results.

claims.text: On Facebook during the 2020 US election, audiences for political news were highly segregated by ideology. Most content that fact-checkers rated false circulated among sources read almost entirely by conservatives.
claims.note: Based on aggregated data for 208 million US users, in a study run with Meta. It covers one platform, one country and one election.

quotes.text: We show that (i) ideological segregation is high and increases as we shift from potential exposure to actual exposure to engagement; (ii) there is an asymmetry between conservative and liberal audiences, with a substantial corner of the news ecosystem consumed exclusively by conservatives; and (iii) most misinformation, as identified by Meta’s Third-Party Fact-Checking Program, exists within this homogeneously conservative corner, which has no equivalent on the liberal side.

claims.text: Switching users from Facebook's and Instagram's ranking algorithms to a newest-first feed cut the time they spent on the platforms and changed what they saw, but did not measurably change their political attitudes over three months.
claims.note: A randomised experiment during the 2020 US election, run with Meta's cooperation. It cannot show what years of exposure do.

quotes.text: Moving users out of algorithmic feeds substantially decreased the time they spent on the platforms and their activity.

Despite these substantial changes in users’ on-platform experience, the chronological feed did not significantly alter levels of issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the 3-month study period.

debates.question: Do social media platforms make people more polarised?
debates.agreed: Platforms change what people see and how long they spend looking. The dispute is whether that changes their political attitudes.

positions.label: Leaving the platform reduces polarisation
positions.text: Allcott and colleagues ran a randomised experiment in which US users deactivated Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 midterm elections. Both political polarisation and knowledge of the news fell.

quotes.text: In a randomized experiment, we find that deactivating Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm election (i) reduced online activity, while increasing offline activities such as watching TV alone and socializing with family and friends; (ii) reduced both factual news knowledge and political polarization

positions.label: Changing the algorithm does not
positions.text: Guess and colleagues found that replacing the ranking algorithm with a newest-first feed left polarisation, political knowledge and other attitudes unchanged over three months.

quotes.text: the chronological feed did not significantly alter levels of issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the 3-month study period.

agreedQuotes.text: Moving users out of algorithmic feeds substantially decreased the time they spent on the platforms and their activity. The chronological feed also affected exposure to content

summaryQuotes.text: Despite these substantial changes in users’ on-platform experience, the chronological feed did not significantly alter levels of issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the 3-month study period.
We compared the inventory of all political news that users could have seen in their feeds with the information that they saw (after algorithmic curation) and the information with which they engaged.

surveillance-digital-rights.title: Surveillance and digital rights
surveillance-digital-rights.summary: Governments of every kind now use digital tools to watch and identify people, and many restrict what can be said and seen online. The same technologies have lawful uses, so the questions are about limits and oversight.

claims.text: Global internet freedom has declined for 15 years in a row. In the latest assessment, conditions worsened in 28 of 72 countries and improved in 17.
claims.note: Freedom House scores countries on access, censorship and violations of users' rights. The scores rest on expert assessment, so the method involves judgement.

quotes.text: Global internet freedom declined for the 15th consecutive year. Of the 72 countries assessed in Freedom on the Net 2025, conditions deteriorated in 28, while 17 countries registered overall gains.

claims.text: By 2019 at least 75 of 176 countries were using AI for surveillance, including facial recognition in 64. Democracies were among the main users: about half of advanced democracies had deployed these systems.
claims.note: Compiled from public reporting, so it probably undercounts. The index does not separate lawful from unlawful use.

quotes.text: At least seventy-five out of 176 countries globally are actively using AI technologies for surveillance purposes. This includes: smart city/safe city platforms (fifty-six countries), facial recognition systems (sixty-four countries), and smart policing (fifty-two countries).
Liberal democracies are major users of AI surveillance. The index shows that 51 percent of advanced democracies deploy AI surveillance systems.

summaryQuotes.text: At least seventy-five out of 176 countries globally are actively using AI technologies for surveillance purposes.

Authorities in these settings expanded restrictions on content, escalated surveillance of electronic communications, and imposed more severe penalties on those who expressed dissent online, particularly during protests and elections.

migration-displacement.title: Migration and displacement
migration-displacement.summary: More people are displaced from their homes than at any time on record. Most stay inside their own country or in a neighbouring one. War and violence are the main causes of lasting displacement; disasters force many more short-term moves.

claims.text: At the end of 2024, 123.2 million people worldwide were forcibly displaced by conflict, persecution or violence.
claims.note: UNHCR's count, drawn from governments, UN agencies and partners. It rose by about 7 million in a year.

claims.text: Most displaced people do not travel far. About 60% are displaced inside their own country, and 73% of refugees are hosted in low- and middle-income countries.
claims.note: 73.5 million of the 123.2 million were internally displaced. Two-thirds of refugees live in a country neighbouring their own.

claims.text: Disasters caused 45.8 million displacements inside countries in 2024, the most since records began in 2008.
claims.note: A displacement is a movement, not a person, and many were planned evacuations. Most people returned home; about 9.8 million were still displaced by disasters at the end of the year.

quotes.text: Nearly 45.8 million disaster displacements were recorded across 163 countries and territories last year, the highest figure since IDMC started to monitor the phenomenon in 2008.

debates.question: How many people will climate change force to move?
debates.agreed: Climate change affects people's livelihoods and where they can live. Most movement linked to it happens within countries.

positions.label: Up to 216 million by 2050
positions.text: The World Bank's Groundswell report finds that climate change could force 216 million people in six regions to move within their own countries by 2050. It adds that decisive collective action could cut this by as much as 80%.

quotes.text: The World Bank’s updated Groundswell report released today finds that climate change, an increasingly potent driver of migration, could force 216 million people across six world regions to move within their countries by 2050.
quotes.where: World Bank press release on the report, 13 September 2021

quotes.text: Decisive collective action could reduce climate migration by as much as 80 percent
quotes.where: World Bank press release on the report, 13 September 2021

positions.label: Mass-migration forecasts are misleading
positions.text: Boas and colleagues argue that predictions of mass climate migration rest on simplistic assumptions and present migration as a security threat without a sound empirical basis. They call for research on how people actually move, stay and adapt.

quotes.text: Misleading claims about mass migration induced by climate change continue to surface in both academia and policy. This requires a new research agenda on ‘climate mobilities’ that moves beyond simplistic assumptions and more accurately advances knowledge of the nexus between human mobility and climate change.
entrenching climate migration as a looming security crisis without an empirical scientific basis
quotes.where: p. 902; quoted from the authors' open-access copy

agreedQuotes.text: the potential for climate change to disrupt livelihoods and threaten lives is real
agreedQuotes.where: p. 901 (opening section); quoted from the authors' open-access copy

agreedQuotes.text: could force 216 million people across six world regions to move within their countries by 2050.
agreedQuotes.where: World Bank press release on the report, 13 September 2021

summaryQuotes.text: This 10th edition of the Global Report on Internal Displacement (GRID) once again presents record-breaking figures, with a global estimate of 83.4 million people living in internal displacement at the end of 2024

food-water-systems.title: Food and water systems
food-water-systems.summary: The way the world grows and eats food drives a large share of both climate change and nature loss. At the same time hundreds of millions of people go hungry and billions lack safe water.

claims.text: About 673 million people, roughly 8% of the world, faced hunger in 2024. The number fell slightly for a second year but rose in Africa and western Asia.
claims.note: The UN agencies give a range of 638 to 720 million.

claims.text: 2.6 billion people could not afford a healthy diet in 2024.
claims.note: Same report. The global number has fallen since 2019 but has risen in low-income countries.

claims.text: 2.1 billion people, one in four, lack safely managed drinking water.
claims.note: The WHO and UNICEF monitoring programme defines this as water on the premises, available when needed and free from contamination.

quotes.text: 1 in 4 – or 2.1 billion people globally – still lack access to safely managed drinking water
quotes.where: WHO and UNICEF news release on the report, 26 August 2025

debates.question: Can everyone eat a diet that is healthy for people and the planet?
debates.agreed: Food systems put heavy pressure on both health and the environment, and most diets today are far from what the EAT–Lancet Commission recommends.

positions.label: Yes, with big changes to diets, waste and farming
positions.text: The EAT–Lancet Commission set out a reference diet for health. It concluded that food systems could provide this diet for nearly 10 billion people by 2050 and stay within safe environmental limits.

quotes.text: food systems can potentially provide the healthy diets (i.e. reference diet) for an anticipated world population of nearly 10 billion people by 2050 and still stay within a safe operating space on Earth.
quotes.where: Quoted from the authors' accepted manuscript, PDF page 5; wording in the published version may differ slightly

positions.label: Not at today's prices and incomes
positions.text: Hirvonen and colleagues priced the cheapest version of that diet in 159 countries at a median of $2.84 a day in 2011. That is more than the whole household income per person of at least 1.58 billion people.

quotes.text: The most affordable EAT–Lancet diets cost a global median of US$2·84 per day (IQR 2·41–3·16) in 2011
We estimated that the cost of an EAT–Lancet diet exceeded household per capita income for at least 1·58 billion people.

agreedQuotes.text: Current diets differ greatly from EAT–Lancet targets.

summaryQuotes.text: In 2015, food-system emissions amounted to 18 Gt CO2 equivalent per year globally, representing 34% of total GHG emissions.
1 in 4 – or 2.1 billion people globally – still lack access to safely managed drinking water
summaryQuotes.where: WHO and UNICEF news release on the report, 26 August 2025

health-pandemics.title: Health and pandemics
health-pandemics.summary: Most new infectious diseases reach people from animals, and the conditions that favour this are spreading. Climate change adds direct harms to health, such as extreme heat. How people respond depends partly on what information they trust.

claims.text: Of 335 infectious diseases that emerged in people between 1940 and 2004, about 60% came from animals, and about 72% of those came from wildlife.
claims.note: A widely cited analysis in Nature. New diseases are more likely to be reported where there is more research, which the authors adjusted for.

quotes.text: Here we analyse a database of 335 EID ‘events’ (origins of EIDs) between 1940 and 2004
EID events are dominated by zoonoses (60.3% of EIDs): the majority of these (71.8%) originate in wildlife

claims.text: An estimated 631,000 to 827,000 viruses not yet discovered in mammals and birds could be able to infect people.
claims.note: An expert estimate extrapolated from limited sampling, published in an IPBES workshop report that was peer-reviewed but not approved by member governments.

quotes.text: An estimated 1.7 million currently undiscovered viruses are thought to exist in mammal and avian hosts. Of these, 631,000-827,000 could have the ability to infect humans.

debates.question: What kind of online content does most to reduce vaccination?
debates.agreed: Seeing false claims about vaccines makes people less willing to be vaccinated.

positions.label: Outright misinformation
positions.text: In a randomised trial in the UK and US in September 2020, Loomba and colleagues found that seeing recent misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines cut the share of people who would definitely accept a vaccine by 6.2 percentage points in the UK and 6.4 in the US.

quotes.text: we conducted a randomized controlled trial in the UK and the USA to quantify how exposure to online misinformation around COVID-19 vaccines affects intent to vaccinate to protect oneself or others.

relative to factual information, recent misinformation induced a decline in intent of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (95th percentile interval 4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.

positions.label: Misleading but not false stories, because far more people see them
positions.text: Allen, Watts and Rand found that content flagged as false was more persuasive per view but was rarely seen. They estimate that unflagged vaccine-sceptical content, including widely viewed stories about rare deaths after vaccination, had 46 times the impact on vaccination intentions on Facebook.

quotes.text: We estimate that the impact of unflagged content that nonetheless encouraged vaccine skepticism was 46-fold greater than that of misinformation flagged by fact-checkers. Although misinformation reduced predicted vaccination intentions significantly more than unflagged vaccine content when viewed, Facebook users’ exposure to flagged content was limited. In contrast, unflagged stories highlighting rare deaths after vaccination were among Facebook’s most-viewed stories.

agreedQuotes.text: relative to factual information, recent misinformation induced a decline in intent of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (95th percentile interval 4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.
misinformation reduced predicted vaccination intentions significantly more than unflagged vaccine content when viewed

summaryQuotes.text: EID events are dominated by zoonoses (60.3% of EIDs): the majority of these (71.8%) originate in wildlife (for example, severe acute respiratory virus, Ebola virus), and are increasing significantly over time.
Land-use change is a globally significant driver of pandemics and caused the emergence of more than 30% of new diseases reported since 1960.
Failure to curb the warming effects of climate change has seen the rate of heat-related deaths surge 23% since the 1990s, to 546,000 a year.

climate-ecology.label: Each makes the other worse
climate-ecology.text: Climate change is the third-largest direct cause of nature loss so far. In the other direction, land and ocean ecosystems absorb the equivalent of roughly 60% of human-caused emissions, so damaging them weakens a natural brake on warming.

quotes.text: The direct drivers of change in nature with the largest global impact have been (starting with those with most impact): changes in land and sea use; direct exploitation of organisms; climate change; pollution; and invasion of alien species.
quotes.where: Summary for Policymakers, key message B

quotes.text: Marine and terrestrial ecosystems are the sole sinks for anthropogenic carbon emissions, with a gross sequestration of 5.6 gigatons of carbon per year (the equivalent of some 60 per cent of global anthropogenic emissions).
quotes.where: Summary for Policymakers, key message A

ai-climate.label: Rising electricity demand
ai-climate.text: Data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of the global total. The IEA projects this will more than double by 2030, with AI the main driver. That is about a tenth of the growth in world electricity demand, and the effects are much larger in the places where data centres cluster.

quotes.text: Data centres accounted for around 1.5% of the world’s electricity consumption in 2024, or 415 terawatt-hours (TWh).

Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh by 2030. This is slightly more than Japan’s total electricity consumption today. AI is the most important driver of this growth
Data centres account for around one-tenth of global electricity demand growth to 2030
The sector accounts for substantial shares of electricity consumption in local markets.

farright-climate.label: Hostility to climate policy
farright-climate.text: Right-wing populist leaders and supporters tend to be sceptical of climate science and hostile to climate policy. A study of OECD countries from 2007 to 2018 found a large negative effect on climate policy when these parties are in power. It found no overall effect on renewable energy policy.

quotes.text: The rise of right-wing populism (RWP) poses a challenge for the climate agenda, as leaders and supporters tend to be climate sceptics and hostile to policy prescribing action on climate change.
we find evidence for a significant and large negative effect of RWPPs in power on climate policy.
In contrast to climate policy, there is no overall significant relationship with renewable policy.

misinfo-climate.label: The consensus gap
misinfo-climate.text: More than 99% of peer-reviewed climate papers agree that humans are causing climate change. Yet a 2016 Pew survey cited in the same study found that only 27% of US adults thought almost all scientists agreed. This entry records the gap. Organised climate obstruction covers one documented source of public doubt.

quotes.text: We conclude with high statistical confidence that the scientific consensus on human-caused contemporary climate change—expressed as a proportion of the total publications—exceeds 99% in the peer reviewed scientific literature.
In 2016 Pew Research found that only 27% of U.S. adults believed that ‘almost all’ scientists agreed that climate change is due to human activity

ai-misinfo.label: More convincing fakes
ai-misinfo.text: AI-generated content is becoming harder to tell apart from real content, and in experiments it can change people's beliefs as effectively as content written by people. Real-world use of AI for manipulation is documented but not yet widespread, and manipulation can be difficult to detect.

quotes.text: AI-generated content has become harder to distinguish from real content.

In experimental settings, AI-generated content can be as effective as human-written content at changing people's beliefs. Real-world use of AI for manipulation is documented but not yet widespread, though it may increase as capabilities improve.
Manipulation can be difficult to detect in practice, making it challenging to prevent through training, monitoring, or safeguards.

farright-misinfo.label: Control of information
farright-misinfo.text: Censoring the media is the most common tactic of governments moving toward autocracy. V-Dem records it in 32 of the 44 countries currently autocratising.

quotes.text: Media censorship remains the most common tactic among autocratizing governments with 32 countries (73%) resorting to it.

inequality-climate.label: Unequal emissions
inequality-climate.text: In 2019 the top 10% of emitters produced 48% of the world's greenhouse gas emissions and the bottom half produced 12%. Most of the gap is now between high and low emitters inside countries, not between countries.

quotes.text: I find that the bottom 50% of the world population emitted 12% of global emissions in 2019, whereas the top 10% emitted 48% of the total.
63% of the global inequality in individual emissions is now due to a gap between low and high emitters within countries rather than between countries.

inequality-farright.label: Economic shocks and backlash
inequality-farright.text: Rodrik's review finds compelling evidence that economic shocks from globalisation have raised support for populist movements, particularly on the right. It also finds that these shocks often work through culture and identity.

quotes.text: There is compelling evidence that globalization shocks, often working through culture and identity, have played an important role in driving up support for populist movements, particularly of the right-wing kind.

obstruction-climate.label: Accurate science, public doubt
obstruction-climate.text: From the late 1970s ExxonMobil's scientists correctly projected warming of about 0.2°C per decade. The study's authors conclude that the company's public statements contradicted its own data, including by overstating how uncertain the science was.

quotes.text: ExxonMobil’s average projected warming was 0.20° ± 0.04°C per decade, which is, within uncertainty, the same as that of independent academic and government projections published between 1970 and 2007.
On each of these points, however, the company’s public statements about climate science contradicted its own scientific data.
ExxonMobil worked to deny it—including overemphasizing uncertainties, denigrating climate models, mythologizing global cooling

obstruction-misinfo.label: Doubt as a strategy
obstruction-misinfo.text: Supran and Oreskes found that the more public an ExxonMobil document was, the more doubt it expressed about climate science. They conclude that the company misled the public.

quotes.text: In all four cases, we find that as documents become more publicly accessible, they increasingly communicate doubt.
Given this discrepancy, we conclude that ExxonMobil misled the public.

polarisation-farright.label: Party before principle
polarisation-farright.text: In a US experiment, only a small fraction of voters put democratic principles first when a candidate they otherwise favoured took an undemocratic position. The stronger voters' partisanship and the further apart the candidates' policies, the less they punished it.

quotes.text: only a small fraction of Americans prioritize democratic principles in their electoral choices, and their tendency to do so is decreasing in several measures of polarization, including the strength of partisanship, policy extremism, and candidate platform divergence.

polarisation-climate.label: Politics predicts climate belief
polarisation-climate.text: A meta-analysis of 25 polls and 171 studies across 56 countries found that political affiliation was the largest demographic correlate of whether people accept that climate change is happening. Education, sex and experience of extreme weather mattered much less than values and political outlook.

quotes.text: Twenty-seven variables were examined by synthesizing 25 polls and 171 academic studies across 56 nations.

many intuitively appealing variables (such as education, sex, subjective knowledge, and experience of extreme weather events) were overshadowed in predictive power by values, ideologies, worldviews and political orientation.
The largest demographic correlate of climate change belief is political affiliation.
quotes.where: Results; quoted from the authors' accepted manuscript, PDF page 4

polarisation-platform.label: Do feeds divide us?
polarisation-platform.text: Experiments point in different directions. Leaving Facebook for four weeks lowered one measure of polarisation, while changing how the feed is ranked did not shift attitudes. The debate under Platform and media power sets out both.

quotes.text: deactivating Facebook for the four weeks before the 2018 US midterm election (i) reduced online activity, while increasing offline activities such as watching TV alone and socializing with family and friends; (ii) reduced both factual news knowledge and political polarization
the chronological feed did not significantly alter levels of issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the 3-month study period.

platform-misinfo.label: Where false stories circulate
platform-misinfo.text: Most content that fact-checkers rated false on Facebook in 2020 sat in one corner of the news ecosystem, with an almost entirely conservative audience. In a separate experiment, removing the ranking algorithm increased the amount of untrustworthy content users saw.

quotes.text: most misinformation, as identified by Meta’s Third-Party Fact-Checking Program, exists within this homogeneously conservative corner, which has no equivalent on the liberal side.
The amount of political and untrustworthy content they saw increased on both platforms

surveillance-ai.label: AI-powered monitoring
surveillance-ai.text: Facial recognition, smart-city platforms and smart policing are the main AI surveillance tools governments use. As of 2019, Chinese companies supplied them to 63 countries and US companies to 32.

quotes.text: This includes: smart city/safe city platforms (fifty-six countries), facial recognition systems (sixty-four countries), and smart policing (fifty-two countries).
Technology linked to Chinese companies—particularly Huawei, Hikvision, Dahua, and ZTE—supply AI surveillance technology in sixty-three countries
AI surveillance technology supplied by U.S. firms is present in thirty-two countries.

surveillance-farright.label: Tools for staying in power
surveillance-farright.text: In China, local governments bought more facial-recognition technology after episodes of unrest, and this suppressed later unrest. Freedom House reports that the governments with the steepest long-term declines in internet freedom expanded surveillance and censorship, particularly around protests and elections.

quotes.text: local unrest leads to greater government procurement of facial-recognition AI as a new technology of political control, and increased AI procurement indeed suppresses subsequent unrest.

Authorities in these settings expanded restrictions on content, escalated surveillance of electronic communications, and imposed more severe penalties on those who expressed dissent online, particularly during protests and elections.

migration-climate.label: Disasters displace millions
migration-climate.text: Disasters caused a record 45.8 million displacements within countries in 2024. More than three-quarters of people displaced by conflict live in countries that are highly vulnerable to climate change.

quotes.text: Nearly 45.8 million disaster displacements were recorded across 163 countries and territories last year, the highest figure since IDMC started to monitor the phenomenon in 2008.
more than three-quarters of people internally displaced by conflict and violence as of the end of 2024 were living in countries with high or very high vulnerability to climate change.

migration-farright.label: Arrivals and hostility
migration-farright.text: On Greek islands that received large numbers of refugees in 2015–16, residents became lastingly more hostile to refugees, immigrants and Muslims, and more supportive of restrictive policies, than residents of similar islands nearby. The refugees were only passing through, so the authors conclude that exposure alone was enough.

quotes.text: we find that direct exposure to refugee arrivals induces sizable and lasting increases in natives’ hostility toward refugees, immigrants, and Muslim minorities; support for restrictive asylum and immigration policies; and political engagement to effect such exclusionary policies. Since refugees only passed through these islands, our findings challenge both standard economic and cultural explanations of anti-immigrant sentiment and show that mere exposure suffices in generating lasting increases in hostility.

food-climate.label: A third of emissions
food-climate.text: Food systems produced 34% of the world's greenhouse gas emissions in 2015. About 71% of that came from farming and land-use change, and the rest from supply-chain activities such as retail, transport, processing, packaging and waste.

quotes.text: In 2015, food-system emissions amounted to 18 Gt CO2 equivalent per year globally, representing 34% of total GHG emissions. The largest contribution came from agriculture and land use/land-use change activities (71%), with the remaining were from supply chain activities: retail, transport, consumption, fuel production, waste management, industrial processes and packaging.

food-ecology.label: Farming drives nature loss
food-ecology.text: Agriculture is an identified threat to 24,000 of the 28,000 species assessed as at risk of extinction, about 86%. The Chatham House report behind this figure names three levers: changing diets, protecting land for nature, and farming in more nature-friendly ways.

health-ecology.label: Spillover from wildlife
health-ecology.text: Land-use change, farm expansion and urban growth cause more than 30% of new disease events, according to an IPBES expert review. Most new infectious diseases come from animals, mainly wildlife.

quotes.text: Land-use change, agricultural expansion, and urbanization cause more than 30% of emerging disease events

health-misinfo.label: Vaccine doubts
health-misinfo.text: In a UK and US trial, seeing recent online misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines cut the share of people who would definitely accept one by about 6 percentage points. Later work estimates that vaccine-sceptical content never flagged as false had far more impact overall, because far more people saw it.

quotes.text: recent misinformation induced a decline in intent of 6.2 percentage points (95th percentile interval 3.9 to 8.5) in the UK and 6.4 percentage points (95th percentile interval 4.0 to 8.8) in the USA among those who stated that they would definitely accept a vaccine.
We estimate that the impact of unflagged content that nonetheless encouraged vaccine skepticism was 46-fold greater than that of misinformation flagged by fact-checkers.
